Finding the Perfect Moto Touring Tent

The tent is the single biggest piece of camping gear you will carry, and choosing the right one is critical. Too heavy and it eats into your payload allowance. Too flimsy and a Scottish mountain wind will collapse it at 3am. The ideal motorcycle touring tent balances weight, packed size, weather resistance, and livability for a realistic price.

What to Look For

  • Weight — Under 2kg for solo riders, under 2.5kg for two-person tents. Every gram counts when it shares pannier space with your riding gear.
  • Packed size — Must fit in or strap onto a pannier. Look for tents that pack to under 45cm long and 15cm diameter.
  • Waterproofing — Minimum 3,000mm HH flysheet and 5,000mm HH groundsheet for British conditions. Taped seams throughout.
  • Wind resistance — Geodesic or semi-geodesic designs handle wind better than simple A-frame tents. Scottish and coastal sites can be extremely exposed.
  • Vestibule — A covered porch area is essential for storing boots and cooking in rain without bringing wet gear inside.

Best Tents for Motorcycle Touring

MSR Hubba Hubba NX — The benchmark lightweight touring tent. Two-person freestanding design at 1.72kg. Two doors and two vestibules give excellent access and storage. Handles wind and rain impressively for its weight.

Vango Blade 100 — A budget-friendly solo tent at 1.95kg with good weather protection. The single hoop design pitches quickly and the vestibule stores boots and cooking gear.

Naturehike Cloud Up 2 — Remarkable value ultralight tent at 1.7kg for a two-person design. Silnylon flysheet is waterproof and packs incredibly small. The interior space is adequate for one rider plus gear.

Robens Voyager Versa 3 — A three-season tunnel tent with excellent storm resistance. Slightly heavier at 2.2kg but the stability in high winds is worth the extra grams for exposed Scottish camping.

Always pitch your tent on the sheltered side of any natural windbreak — a wall, hedge, or tree line. Even the best tent benefits from protection against prevailing wind, which in the UK typically comes from the south-west.

Tent Care on Tour

Pack your tent dry whenever possible. If you must pack it wet, pitch it to dry at your next stop. Prolonged storage while damp leads to mildew which degrades waterproof coatings. Clean the groundsheet of debris before packing and never store the tent compressed long-term — let it breathe between trips.

Freestanding vs Non-Freestanding

Freestanding tents pitch without stakes, useful on hard ground. Non-freestanding tents require stakes but are often lighter. For UK touring where campsite ground varies from soft grass to hard-packed gravel, freestanding designs offer more versatility.

faq.q: How light should a motorcycle touring tent be?
faq.a: Aim for under 2kg for a solo tent and under 2.5kg for a two-person design, packing to under about 45cm long and 15cm diameter so it fits in or straps onto a pannier. Every gram counts when the tent shares pannier space with your riding gear, but do not sacrifice weather protection for the sake of shaving off a few hundred grams.

faq.q: What waterproof rating do I need for the UK?
faq.a: For British conditions, look for a minimum 3000mm hydrostatic head on the flysheet and 5000mm on the groundsheet, with taped seams throughout. Anything less struggles in sustained rain and prolonged ground moisture. The groundsheet rating matters especially, because you are lying on it and body weight forces water through a weak groundsheet.

Freestanding tents pitch without stakes, which is useful on hard or rocky ground where pegs will not bite. Non-freestanding tents need staking but are often lighter. For UK touring where campsite ground varies from soft grass to hard-packed gravel, a freestanding design offers more versatility and is easier to reposition once pitched.

faq.q: How do I pitch a tent in strong wind?
faq.a: Pitch on the sheltered side of a natural windbreak such as a wall, hedge or tree line, with the low end or the strongest pole geometry facing the prevailing wind, which in the UK usually comes from the south-west. Peg out every guy line properly. A geodesic or semi-geodesic tent copes far better with exposed Scottish and coastal pitches than a simple hoop or A-frame.

faq.q: How do I care for my tent on tour?
faq.a: Pack the tent dry whenever possible. If you must pack it wet, pitch it to dry at your next stop, because prolonged damp storage breeds mildew that degrades the waterproof coatings. Clear debris from the groundsheet before packing, and between trips store the tent loosely rather than tightly compressed so the fabric can breathe.
